The Long History of the Bicycle

By Ada Reporter

The bicycle is one of the most efficient machines ever built, converting human effort into motion with very little wasted energy. Its story begins in 1817, when the German inventor Karl Drais unveiled a wooden two-wheeled machine that riders pushed along with their feet. Called the draisine or running machine, it had no pedals, no chain and no brakes, yet it let a person travel far faster than walking. Within a few years the idea had spread across Europe and America, improved with iron frames and better steering, and it set the basic layout that every bicycle since has followed: two wheels in line, steered at the front.

Pedals arrived in the 1860s, attached directly to the front wheel of the machine the French called the velocipede and everyone else called the boneshaker, for its iron tyres on cobbled streets. To go faster, makers simply enlarged the front wheel, which produced the famous penny-farthing of the 1870s, with a front wheel as tall as its rider. These machines were fast but dangerous: a sudden stop could pitch the rider headfirst over the handlebars, an accident known grimly as a header. Cycling in this era was a sport for athletic young men, not a practical way for ordinary people to travel.

The breakthrough came in 1885, when John Kemp Starley of Coventry introduced the Rover safety bicycle. The safety bicycle arrived in 1885 with two wheels of nearly equal size, pedals in the middle driving the rear wheel by a chain, and a frame shape that let the rider put both feet on the ground. It was safer, cheaper and easier to ride than the penny-farthing, and within a decade it had swept the older designs away. Add John Boyd Dunlop's pneumatic tyre in 1888, which replaced bone-jarring solid rubber with a cushion of air, and the modern bicycle was essentially complete.

The 1890s saw a genuine bicycle boom. Factories in England, France, Germany and the United States turned out millions of machines a year, and prices fell until a bicycle cost only a few weeks' wages. For working people the bicycle was the first affordable personal transport: it tripled the distance a person could travel to work, to market or to visit family. For women it was revolutionary. The safety bicycle could be ridden in a long skirt, and later with a dropped frame, and cycling gave many women an experience of unchaperoned freedom that reformers of the day, including the American campaigner Susan B. Anthony, praised as doing more for emancipation than anything else in the world.

The bicycle also changed the world around it. Cyclists demanded better roads long before motorists did, and their clubs lobbied successfully for smooth tarmac surfaces. The bicycle industry pioneered ball bearings, lightweight steel tubing, chain drives and mass-production techniques that the young motor industry borrowed wholesale; several famous car and aviation firms, including the Wright brothers, who ran a bicycle shop in Ohio, began with bicycles. The Wrights used bicycle parts, bicycle chains and their earnings from the shop to build and test the first successful aeroplane in 1903.

In the twentieth century the bicycle's fortunes rose and fell with the car. In Britain and America it became largely a children's toy and a sporting machine after 1950, while in the Netherlands, Denmark and much of Asia it remained everyday transport for millions. The mountain bike, developed in California in the 1970s with fat tyres and low gears, brought a new generation back to cycling for pleasure. Racing machines grew lighter with aluminium and then carbon fibre frames, and gears, brakes and tyres improved beyond anything the Victorians could have imagined.

Today there are an estimated two billion bicycles in the world, more than twice the number of cars. Cities from Copenhagen to Amsterdam organise their streets around them, and bike-sharing schemes have put fleets of identical machines on pavements from Paris to Beijing. The newest chapter is electric assistance: a small motor and battery that help the rider up hills and extend the practical range of a trip. E-bikes now outsell conventional bicycles in several European countries, and delivery riders in crowded cities have adopted them eagerly.

Engineers still return to the bicycle because it remains a benchmark of elegant design. A cyclist on a good machine can travel four times faster than a pedestrian while using no more energy, making the bicycle the most efficient self-powered vehicle known. Its basic design has not changed in more than a century, yet materials, tyres and electrification keep finding new life in it. Two wheels, a chain and a frame: the safety bicycle of 1885 would be instantly recognisable to its inventor, and instantly rideable by almost anyone alive today.
